rv.q: David McVicar's new staging of Puccini's melodramatic thriller, unveiled on New Year's Eve, feels like a course correction—one that is less risky and more successful.
McVicar’s staging is so harmless, with just enough good taste to keep detractors at bay...Still, with the right performers bringing a sense of intimacy to its vast canvas, it feels like a success.
But even with some exciting singing, this “Tosca” could point the company in the wrong direction.
The result was a grand triumph that relegated the old Met Tosca to the list of forgotten flops.

There's nothing wrong with the company's surprise-free new take on one of Italian opera's most famous works that a stronger director couldn't come in and cure because, with Sir David McVicar at the helm, the production didn't get the firm hand that it needed.
That debacle was”redeemed” last night when the company unveiled a listless new production of the melodrama hobbled by inert dramaturgy and slovenly musical values.
There was no mistaking the grittiness of Puccini’s fast-paced thriller at the Metropolitan Opera.
An outstanding performance of convincing dramatic power and elaborate theatrical details.
The production itself proved unable to live up to the hype that its pre-production hinted at.

cn.t: McVicar's sumptuous production overcomes backstage chaos with mixed results—critics praise the traditional staging and strong vocal performances, but some find the direction uninspired and musical execution inconsistent.
